opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For a long time, physical animation, meaning characters whose motion is actually simulated by physics rather than just played back from keyframes, was something only a handful of specialists could do well. You had to hand-tune controllers, adjust gains, write state machines for every gait and recovery, and even then a character would fall over the moment it hit something you didn't anticipate. So most games and films stuck with kinematic animation: motion capture clips blended together. It looks good in the canned cases, but it doesn't really respond to the world. A character can't stumble convincingly, catch itself, or push a heavy door in a way that feels real.

The opportunity I saw is that reinforcement learning and large-scale motion data together change who can make this work and how far it can go. Instead of engineering a controller by hand, you give a simulated character a body, a physics engine, and a big library of human motion, and let it learn a policy that imitates those motions while staying physically valid. Once it has learned that, the character can adapt. Push it and it recovers. Put it on uneven terrain and it adjusts its steps. Ask it to pick up an object it has never seen and it can generalize from what it learned.

Two things made me feel the timing was right. First, GPU-parallel simulation got fast enough to train thousands of characters at once, so what used to take weeks takes hours. Second, generative models showed that you can learn a broad motion prior, not just one skill at a time. Combining a generative motion model with a physics-based controller means you get both diversity and realism, plus the ability to steer the character with high-level commands, even natural language.

And the bigger picture is that this doesn't stop at animation. A character that can control a simulated human body is very close to the same problem as controlling a humanoid robot. The same data, the same simulators, and the same learning methods carry over. So for me, AI-driven physical animation is both a way to make virtual worlds much more alive and interactive, and a stepping stone toward embodied intelligence in the real world. That combination is what made it feel like a really exciting direction to bet on.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the opportunity came from frustration more than from any grand vision.

When I started, physical animation was a very craft-based field. If you wanted a character to walk, jump, or get knocked over and recover, you had two options. You either keyframed it by hand, or you captured a performer and replayed the data. Both approaches share the same weakness: the result only ever does what you recorded. Push the character in a way the animator didn't anticipate and it falls apart. Every new behavior meant another round of capture, cleanup, and tuning. It didn't scale.

Meanwhile, the physics side had been there for decades. We knew how to simulate rigid bodies, contact, friction, muscles even. What we lacked was control. Writing a controller by hand for a simulated humanoid is brutally hard, and every controller was bespoke. A running controller told you nothing about how to build a climbing controller.

What I saw around the time deep reinforcement learning started working was that these two problems were really the same problem. A simulator is an infinite data generator. If you can specify what you want as an objective instead of as a trajectory, the learning algorithm can discover the control strategy itself, and it discovers it inside a world that obeys physics. So the motion you get is responsive by construction. It reacts to perturbations, to terrain, to other characters, because it was learned under those conditions rather than recorded in a studio.

The deeper opportunity, which I only appreciated later, is that animation and robotics were quietly converging. A learned controller for a simulated humanoid and a learned controller for a real humanoid robot are the same object, up to the gap between simulation and reality. So the techniques developed for games and film turned out to be a rehearsal space for embodied intelligence. Animation gave us permission to fail cheaply, millions of times, and that's exactly what learning needs.

So the short answer: the opportunity was to replace recording motion with learning motion, and to turn the simulator from a playback device into a teacher.

astra-6.text:
The opportunity I saw was to make movement something a character could learn, rather than something we had to design for every situation. With traditional animation, you can create beautiful motion, but when the environment changes or the character encounters something unexpected, producing the right response takes a lot of additional work.

Physics gives us a way to make those responses grounded in the world. AI offers a way to learn how to control the movement—how to balance, adapt, and interact. Bringing them together could make characters more responsive while reducing the amount of manual animation needed. That opens up possibilities for much richer interaction.

sol-6.1.text: The opportunity I saw was to move from animating how something looks to learning how it behaves. With traditional animation, you often need a lot of manual work to create a movement and adapt it to different situations. Physics gives you a foundation, but designing a controller that produces natural motion is still difficult. AI offers a way to learn those skills from data, so a character can respond to changes in its environment while remaining physically plausible. That opens up possibilities for more interactive characters, as well as tools that let artists focus more on what they want to express.
